Post 04 ended by building new fields: C=R[x]/(x2+1) and F4=F2[x]/(x2+x+1). This post studies such constructions systematically. A bigger field E containing F is a vector space over F, and its dimension, the degree, turns out to be a very strong invariant: a single divisibility argument proves that no ruler-and-compass construction doubles a cube or trisects a 60° angle. Galois theory then attaches to a polynomial a finite group, the permutations of its roots that respect all algebraic relations, and the Fundamental Theorem matches the subfields of the splitting field with the subgroups of that group. Everything from posts 01–04 comes together here: groups, normal subgroups and quotients, group actions, Sylow-type counting, irreducible polynomials and quotient rings. The chapter ends with the reason there is no quintic formula.
Series map: 00 Integers, Relations & Modular Arithmetic → 01 Groups & Subgroups → 02 Cosets, Lagrange & Quotient Groups → 03 Homomorphisms, Group Actions & Sylow → 04 Rings, Ideals & Fields → 05 Field Extensions & Galois Theory (this post).

Extension — a pair of fields F⊆E, written E/F ("E over F"). F is the base field.
Degree — [E:F]=dim⁡FE, the dimension of E as a vector space over F. The extension is finite if the degree is finite.
Generated extension — for α∈E, F(α) is the smallest subfield of E containing F and α. Likewise F(α1,…,αn). An extension F(α)/F is simple and α is a primitive element.
Intermediate field — a field K with F⊆K⊆E.
Examples: [C:R]=2 with basis 1,i. [Q(2):Q]=2 with basis 1,2, since Q(2)={a+b2:a,b∈Q} and 2∉Q. [R:Q] is infinite (a countable field cannot span the uncountable R with finitely many vectors). A field with q elements that contains Fp has q=pn where n=[E:Fp], because an n-dimensional vector space over Fp has pn elements.

Theorem (tower law). If F⊆K⊆E are fields, then
[E:F]=[E:K] [K:F],
in the sense that the left side is finite exactly when both factors are, and then equality holds.
Proof (finite case). Let α1,…,αm be a basis of K over F and β1,…,βn a basis of E over K. The claim is that the mn products αiβj form a basis of E over F.
Spanning. Any e∈E is ∑jkjβj with kj∈K, and each kj=∑ifijαi with fij∈F. So e=∑i,jfij αiβj.
Independence. If ∑i,jfijαiβj=0, regroup as ∑j(∑ifijαi)βj=0. The inner sums are in K and the βj are independent over K, so each inner sum is 0. The αi are independent over F, so every fij=0. ∎
Corollaries. (1) If K is intermediate in a finite extension E/F, then [K:F] divides [E:F]. (2) If [E:F] is prime, there is no intermediate field other than F and E. (3) If α∈E, then [F(α):F] divides [E:F].
Trick: most degree computations are "bound above by a tower, bound below by divisibility". If [K:F]=2 and [L:F]=3 are both inside E, then 6∣[E:F].

Algebraic — α∈E is algebraic over F if f(α)=0 for some nonzero f∈F[x]. Otherwise α is transcendental over F.
Algebraic extension — every element of E is algebraic over F.
Minimal polynomial — the monic polynomial mα∈F[x] of least degree with mα(α)=0.
2, i, 23 and e2πi/5 are algebraic over Q. Hermite proved in 1873 that e is transcendental and Lindemann in 1882 that π is transcendental; both proofs are analytic and are not needed below.

Theorem. Let α be algebraic over F. Then:
mα exists, is unique, and is irreducible over F;
for f∈F[x]: f(α)=0 if and only if mα∣f;
F(α)≅F[x]/(mα), so [F(α):F]=deg⁡mα, with basis 1,α,…,αn−1 where n=deg⁡mα.
Proof. Evaluation evα:F[x]→E, f↦f(α), is a ring homomorphism. Its kernel I is nonzero because α is algebraic, and F[x] is a PID (post 04), so I=(m) for a unique monic m; this m has least degree among nonzero elements of I, so m=mα, and statement 2 is "f∈I ⟺ mα∣f". The image of evα is a subring of the field E, hence a domain, so by the First Isomorphism Theorem F[x]/(mα) is a domain: (mα) is prime, so mα is irreducible. Then (mα) is maximal (post 04, Chapter 6), so the image F[α] is a field containing F and α; it is therefore F(α). The basis claim is the division algorithm: every class has a unique representative of degree <n. ∎
So to find [F(α):F]: find a polynomial with root α and prove it irreducible with the tests of post 04.
Common pitfall: the minimal polynomial depends on the base field. m2 over Q is x2−2; over R it is x−2.
Arithmetic in Q(23). Let a=23, with ma=x3−2 (Eisenstein at 2), so [Q(a):Q]=3 with basis 1,a,a2. To invert 1+a, use (1+a)(1−a+a2)=1+a3=3:
11+23=1−23+433.
Finite implies algebraic. If [E:F]=n and α∈E, the n+1 elements 1,α,…,αn are linearly dependent over F, and a dependence relation is a nonzero polynomial with root α. Consequently, if α and β are algebraic then F(α,β) is finite (tower law), so α±β, αβ and α/β are algebraic too: the algebraic numbers form a field.

Degree. [Q(2):Q]=2. Next, 3∉Q(2): if (a+b2)2=3 with a,b∈Q, then a2+2b2=3 and 2ab=0. b=0 gives a2=3 and a=0 gives b2=3/2, neither possible in Q. So x2−3 stays irreducible over Q(2), and by the tower law
[Q(2,3):Q]=[Q(2,3):Q(2)] [Q(2):Q]=2⋅2=4,
with basis 1,2,3,6 (products of the two bases, as in the proof of the tower law).
A primitive element. Let θ=2+3. Then θ2=5+26, so (θ2−5)2=24, that is
θ4−10θ2+1=0.
Also θ3=112+93, which gives 2=(θ3−9θ)/2 and 3=(11θ−θ3)/2. So Q(θ) contains 2 and 3, hence Q(θ)=Q(2,3) has degree 4. A degree-4 monic polynomial with root θ must then be the minimal polynomial: mθ=x4−10x2+1, irreducible over Q (its four roots are ±2±3).
This is an instance of the primitive element theorem: every finite separable extension (Chapter 5; in particular every finite extension of Q) is simple.

Start with the points 0 and 1 in the plane C. A ruler draws the line through two constructed points; a compass draws a circle with a constructed centre through a constructed point. New points are intersections of lines and circles. A real number is constructible if it is a coordinate of a constructible point.
Key observation. If all points so far have coordinates in a field K, then:
the intersection of two lines solves a linear system, so it has coordinates in K;
an intersection involving a circle solves a quadratic equation over K, so it has coordinates in K or in some K(d) with d∈K, an extension of degree 2.
Theorem. If α is constructible, then [Q(α):Q] is a power of 2.
Proof. By the observation, α lies in the top field of a tower Q=K0⊂K1⊂⋯⊂Kr with each [Ki+1:Ki]=2. By the tower law [Kr:Q]=2r, and [Q(α):Q] divides it. ∎
Doubling the cube. A cube of volume 2 needs side 23, whose minimal polynomial x3−2 has degree 3. Not a power of 2, so impossible.
Trisecting 60°. A 60° angle is constructible (equilateral triangle). Trisecting it means constructing c=cos⁡20∘. From cos⁡3θ=4cos⁡3θ−3cos⁡θ with θ=20∘ and cos⁡60∘=12:
4c3−3c=12⟺8c3−6c−1=0.
By the rational root test, a rational root would be one of ±1,±12,±14,±18; substituting gives 1,−3,−3,1,−198,38,−11164,−1764, never 0. A cubic without rational roots is irreducible, so [Q(c):Q]=3 and the trisection is impossible. (Some angles,

By the rational root test, a rational root would be one of ±1,±12,±14,±18; substituting gives 1,−3,−3,1,−198,38,−11164,−1764, never 0. A cubic without rational roots is irreducible, so [Q(c):Q]=3 and the trisection is impossible. (Some angles, such as 90°, can be trisected; the theorem is that no method works for every angle.)
Squaring the circle. A square of area π needs side π. If π were constructible it would be algebraic, so π would be algebraic, contradicting Lindemann.
Watch out: "degree a power of 2" is necessary, not sufficient. The exact criterion is that the splitting field of the minimal polynomial has degree a power of 2. The Gauss–Wantzel theorem answers the polygon question: a regular n-gon is constructible if and only if n is a power of 2 times a product of distinct Fermat primes 3,5,17,257,65537.

A splitting field of a nonconstant f∈F[x] is an extension E/F in which f factors into linear factors, f=c(x−α1)⋯(x−αn), and which is generated by the roots: E=F(α1,…,αn).
Theorem. Every nonconstant f∈F[x] has a splitting field E, with [E:F]≤n! where n=deg⁡f. Any two splitting fields of f over F are isomorphic by an isomorphism that fixes F.
(Existence: take an irreducible factor p of f; in F[x]/(p) it has a root (post 04), so f gains a linear factor over an extension of degree ≤n; repeat on the quotient, whose degree is n−1. Uniqueness is proved by the same induction, extending an isomorphism one root at a time.)
Examples:
x2−2 over Q: splitting field Q(2), degree 2.
x4−10x2+1: roots ±2±3, splitting field Q(2,3), degree 4.
x3−2: roots α, αω, αω2 with α=23 and ω=e2πi/3, a root of x2+x+1. The splitting field is E=Q(α,ω) (it contains ω=αω/α). [Q(α):Q]=3, and ω∉Q(α)⊂R, so [E:Q(α)]=2. Hence [E:Q]=6=3!, the maximum.

Let E be a finite field. Its characteristic is a prime p (post 04), so it contains Fp and has pn elements, n=[E:Fp].
Lemma (freshman's dream). In a commutative ring of characteristic p, (a+b)p=ap+bp.
Proof. Expand with the binomial theorem. For 0<k<p, (pk)=p!k!(p−k)! is divisible by p: p divides the numerator but not the denominator. So all middle terms vanish. ∎
Hence the Frobenius map Fr(a)=ap is a ring homomorphism. On a field it is injective (post 04: homomorphisms out of fields are injective), so on a finite field it is an automorphism, and it fixes exactly the elements of Fp (the roots of xp−x; there are at most p of them, and all of Fp qualifies by Fermat's little theorem from post 00).
Theorem (existence and uniqueness of finite fields). For every prime p and n≥1 there is a field with q=pn elements, and any two such fields are isomorphic. It is written Fq.
Proof. Existence. Let E be a splitting field of g=xq−x over Fp, and S the set of roots of g in E. The derivative g′=qxq−1−1=−1 has no common root with g, so the roots are distinct and ∣S∣=q. S is a subfield: if aq=a and bq=b, then (a+b)q=aq+bq=a+b (apply the lemma n times), (ab)q=ab, and (a−1)q=a−1. A subfield containing all roots is the whole splitting field, so E=S has q elements.
Uniqueness. In any field K with q elements, the multiplicative group has order q−1, so aq−1=1 for a≠0 by Lagrange, and aq=a for all a. So

(ab)q=ab, and (a−1)q=a−1. A subfield containing all roots is the whole splitting field, so E=S has q elements.
Uniqueness. In any field K with q elements, the multiplicative group has order q−1, so aq−1=1 for a≠0 by Lagrange, and aq=a for all a. So K consists of the q roots of xq−x, and is a splitting field of xq−x over Fp. Splitting fields are unique up to isomorphism. ∎
Two further facts, stated without proof: the multiplicative group Fq× is cyclic (post 04's F8 table showed a generator), and Fpd sits inside Fpn exactly when d∣n.
Worked example. Over F2:
x4−x=x (x+1) (x2+x+1),x8−x=x (x+1) (x3+x+1) (x3+x2+1).
The first line lists the minimal polynomials of the 4 elements of F4; the second those of the 8 elements of F8. The two cubics are the two irreducible cubics over F2, each with three roots in F8. No quadratic appears in the second line, matching 2∤3: F4⊈F8.

F-automorphism of E — a field automorphism σ:E→E with σ(a)=a for every a∈F. They form a group Aut⁡(E/F).
Fixed field — for a subgroup H≤Aut⁡(E), EH={e∈E:σ(e)=e for all σ∈H}.
Separable polynomial — one with no repeated root in its splitting field. An algebraic extension is separable if every minimal polynomial is separable.
Normal extension — an algebraic E/F such that every irreducible polynomial in F[x] with one root in E splits completely in E.
Galois extension — a finite extension that is normal and separable. Its Galois group is Gal⁡(E/F)=Aut⁡(E/F).
Galois group of a polynomial — Gal⁡(E/F) for E a splitting field of the (separable) polynomial.
Separability is automatic in the cases you meet most. Over a field of characteristic 0, and over any finite field, every irreducible polynomial is separable. (An irreducible f has a repeated root only if gcd⁡(f,f′)≠1, which forces f′=0; in characteristic 0 that is impossible for nonconstant f.) The standard inseparable example is xp−t over the field Fp(t) of rational functions: it is irreducible (Eisenstein at the prime t), but over its splitting field it equals (x−t1/p)p.

Lemma. If f∈F[x], α∈E is a root of f, and σ∈Aut⁡(E/F), then σ(α) is a root of f.
Proof. If f=∑ckxk with ck∈F, then f(σ(α))=∑ckσ(α)k=σ(∑ckαk)=σ(0)=0, since σ fixes each ck. ∎
So if E=F(α1,…,αn) is a splitting field of f, an F-automorphism is determined by how it permutes α1,…,αn, and Aut⁡(E/F) is (isomorphic to) a subgroup of Sn, an action on the roots in the sense of post 03.
Theorem (characterisations of Galois extensions). For a finite extension E/F the following are equivalent:
E/F is Galois (normal and separable);
E is the splitting field over F of a separable polynomial;
∣Aut⁡(E/F)∣=[E:F];
the fixed field of Aut⁡(E/F) is exactly F.
In general ∣Aut⁡(E/F)∣≤[E:F] and equality is what "Galois" means in practice.
Examples.
Gal⁡(C/R)={id,complex conjugation}≅Z/2Z.
Q(23)/Q is not Galois. An automorphism must send 23 to a root of x3−2 inside Q(23)⊂R, and the only real root is 23 itself. So Aut⁡ is trivial, of order 1<3. It fails normality: x3−2 has one root in the field but does not split there.
Gal⁡(Fpn/Fp) is cyclic of order n, generated by Frobenius. (Frk fixes exactly the roots of xpk−x, so Fr has order exactly n; and the group has order [Fpn:Fp]=n because Fpn is the splitting field of the separable xpn−x.)

Theorem (Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory). Let E/F be a finite Galois extension with group G=Gal⁡(E/F). Then the maps
H⟼EHandK⟼Gal⁡(E/K)
are mutually inverse bijections between subgroups H≤G and intermediate fields F⊆K⊆E, and:
they reverse inclusion: H1≤H2 if and only if EH1⊇EH2;
degrees match indices: [E:EH]=∣H∣ and [EH:F]=[G:H];
K/F is Galois if and only if Gal⁡(E/K) is a normal subgroup of G, and then Gal⁡(K/F)≅G/Gal⁡(E/K).
So the lattice of intermediate fields is the lattice of subgroups turned upside down: the big field E matches the trivial group, the base F matches all of G. Part 3 is where normal subgroups and quotient groups (post 02) acquire their original meaning.

E=Q(2,3) is the splitting field of the separable (x2−2)(x2−3), so it is Galois of degree 4 and G has 4 elements. Each automorphism sends 2↦±2 and 3↦±3, and all four sign choices occur. Let
σ:2↦−2, 3↦3,τ:2↦2, 3↦−3.
Each has order 2 and they commute, so G={id,σ,τ,στ}≅Z/2×Z/2. The subgroups and their fixed fields:
Subgroup · Order · Fixed field · Degree over Q
{id} · 1 · Q(2,3) · 4
⟨σ⟩ · 2 · Q(3) · 2
⟨τ⟩ · 2 · Q(2) · 2
⟨στ⟩ · 2 · Q(6) · 2
G · 4 · Q · 1
(στ(6)=(−2)(−3)=6.) By the theorem these are all the intermediate fields: exactly three quadratic subfields, which is not obvious without Galois theory. G is abelian, so every subgroup is normal and every intermediate field is Galois over Q.

E=Q(α,ω) with α=23, of degree 6 (Chapter 4). It is Galois, so ∣G∣=6, and G acts on the three roots α,αω,αω2, so G is a subgroup of S3 of order 6: G≅S3. Concretely an automorphism is fixed by α↦αωa (a∈{0,1,2}) and ω↦ω or ω2. Let
σ:α↦αω, ω↦ω(order 3),τ:α↦α, ω↦ω2(complex conjugation, order 2).
Composing right to left (apply τ first in στ): στ sends α↦αω and ω↦ω2, so στ(αω2)=αω⋅ω4=αω2. Similarly σ2τ fixes αω. The six subgroups of S3 and their fixed fields:
Subgroup · Order · Normal? · Fixed field · Degree over Q
{id} · 1 · yes · Q(α,ω) · 6
⟨τ⟩ · 2 · no · Q(α) · 3
⟨στ⟩ · 2 · no · Q(αω2) · 3
⟨σ2τ⟩ · 2 · no · Q(αω) · 3
⟨σ⟩=A3 · 3 · yes · Q(ω) · 2
S3 · 6 · yes · Q · 1
Each order-2 subgroup fixes one real or complex cube root, so its fixed field contains that root; the degree count [G:H]=3=[Q(αωk):Q] makes it equal to Q(αωk). σ fixes ω, and [G:⟨σ⟩]=2=[Q(ω):Q].
Part 3 of the theorem, checked on this example: A3=⟨σ⟩ is normal, and Q(ω) is Galois over Q (it is the splitting field of x2+x+1), with Gal⁡(Q(ω)/Q)≅S3/A3≅Z/2. The three subgroups of order 2 are not normal (they are conjugate, like the three Sylow 2-subgroups of S3 in post 03), and correspondingly Q(23) and its two conjugate fields are not Galois over Q.
Common pitfall: the correspondence reverses order. A bigger subgroup fixes more conditions and so has a smaller fixed field. Draw the two lattices with E at the top and {id} at the top.

A group G is solvable if there is a chain of subgroups
{e}=G0⊴G1⊴⋯⊴Gk=G
with each Gi normal in Gi+1 and each quotient Gi+1/Gi abelian.
Abelian groups are solvable (k=1).
S3: {e}⊴A3⊴S3 with quotients Z/3 and Z/2.
S4: {e}⊴V4⊴A4⊴S4 with quotients Z/2×Z/2, Z/3, Z/2. So every subgroup of S4 is solvable too (subgroups and quotients of solvable groups are solvable).
S5 is not solvable. Its only normal subgroups are {e}, A5, S5, and A5 is simple and non-abelian (post 02). A chain would have to pass through A5, and the step below A5 would need a normal subgroup of A5 with abelian quotient; the only candidates are A5 itself (quotient trivial, no progress) and {e} (quotient A5, not abelian). Equivalently, the commutator subgroup of A5 is A5, so the derived series S5⊃A5⊃A5⊃⋯ never reaches {e}.

A polynomial f∈Q[x] is solvable by radicals if its roots can be written starting from rational numbers using +,−,×,÷ and k-th roots. The quadratic formula shows this for degree 2; Cardano's and Ferrari's formulas do it for degrees 3 and 4.
Theorem (Galois, characteristic 0). f is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is solvable.
(Idea of "only if": adjoining a k-th root to a field that already contains the k-th roots of unity gives a Galois extension with cyclic group; adjoining roots of unity gives an abelian group. A tower of such steps gives, through part 3 of the Fundamental Theorem, a chain of normal subgroups with abelian quotients.)
Since S4 is solvable and the Galois group of a degree-n polynomial embeds in Sn, every polynomial of degree ≤4 is solvable by radicals. The Abel–Ruffini theorem says the general quintic is not: the generic polynomial x5+a4x4+⋯+a0 with independent indeterminate coefficients has Galois group S5 over Q(a0,…,a4), which is not solvable, so there is no formula in radicals valid for all quintics. Galois theory gives more: specific quintics with rational coefficients have unsolvable roots.

Lemma. Let p be prime and f∈Q[x] irreducible of degree p with exactly two non-real roots. Then Gal⁡(f)≅Sp.
Proof. View G=Gal⁡(f) as a subgroup of Sp acting on the p roots. For a root α, [Q(α):Q]=p divides [E:Q]=∣G∣, so by Cauchy's theorem (post 03) G has an element of order p; in Sp the elements of order p are the p-cycles. Complex conjugation restricts to an element of G that swaps the two non-real roots and fixes the p−2 real ones: a transposition. For prime p, a p-cycle and a transposition generate all of Sp. ∎
Theorem. f(x)=x5−4x+2 is not solvable by radicals over Q.
Proof. Irreducible: Eisenstein at p=2 (2∣−4, 2∣2, 4∤2, leading coefficient 1).
Exactly three real roots: f′(x)=5x4−4 vanishes only at x=±c with c=(4/5)1/4≈0.9457. So f increases, then decreases on [−c,c], then increases. The local maximum f(−c)≈5.03>0 and the local minimum f(c)≈−1.03<0, while f→−∞ as x→−∞ and f→+∞ as x→+∞. So f crosses zero once on each of the three monotone pieces: three real roots, approximately −1.5185, 0.5085 and 1.2436, and the other two roots are a complex-conjugate pair.
By the lemma with p=5, Gal⁡(f)≅S5, which is not solvable. By Galois's theorem, f is not solvable by radicals. ∎
Watch out: "not solvable by radicals" does not mean the roots are hard to compute. Numerically they are easy (the values above). It means there is no finite expression in +,−,×,÷, k for them.

1. Find [Q(2,23):Q].
Solution
Q(2) has degree 2 and Q(23) has degree 3, both intermediate, so 2 and 3 divide the degree, and so does 6. On the other hand [Q(2,23):Q(23)]≤2 (root of x2−2), so the degree is at most 2⋅3=6. Hence it is exactly 6.
2. Find the minimal polynomial of 2+i over Q.
Solution
Let θ=2+i. Then θ2=1+22 i, so (θ2−1)2=−8, giving θ4−2θ2+9=0. As in the 2+3 example, Q(θ)=Q(2,i), which has degree 4 (i∉Q(2)⊂R). So mθ=x4−2x2+9.
3. Show that the regular 7-gon is not constructible, using that 2cos⁡(2π/7) is a root of x3+x2−2x−1.
Solution
Rational roots could only be ±1, which give −1 and 1, so the cubic has no rational root and is irreducible. Then [Q(2cos⁡(2π/7)):Q]=3, not a power of 2, so cos⁡(2π/7) is not constructible, and neither is the 7-gon. (Consistent with Gauss–Wantzel: 7 is prime but not a Fermat prime.)
4. List all subfields of F64 and draw their inclusions. What is Gal⁡(F64/F2)?
Solution
64=26 and the divisors of 6 are 1, 2, 3, 6, so the subfields are F2,F4,F8,F64. Inclusions: F2⊂F4⊂F64 and F2⊂F8⊂F64, while F4⊈F8. The Galois group is cyclic of order 6, generated by Frobenius; its subgroups (orders 1, 2, 3, 6) match the subfields F64,F8,F4,F2 in that order.
5. In Q(2,3), which automorphism fixes 6, and what is the fixed field of {id,σ}? Why does the Fundamental Theorem guarantee that Q(2+3) is the whole field without computing θ3?
Solution
στ fixes 6 (both

the subfields F64,F8,F4,F2 in that order.
5. In Q(2,3), which automorphism fixes 6, and what is the fixed field of {id,σ}? Why does the Fundamental Theorem guarantee that Q(2+3) is the whole field without computing θ3?
Solution
στ fixes 6 (both signs flip). σ fixes 3, so E⟨σ⟩⊇Q(3), and both have degree 2, so they are equal. For θ=2+3: the non-identity automorphisms send θ to −2+3, 2−3, −2−3, all different from θ. So only the trivial subgroup fixes θ, and Q(θ) corresponds to {id}, i.e. it is all of E.
6. Explain why every polynomial of degree at most 4 over Q is solvable by radicals, but this argument says nothing about degree 5.
Solution
The Galois group of a degree-n polynomial is a subgroup of Sn. For n≤4, Sn is solvable (chains above), and subgroups of solvable groups are solvable, so Galois's theorem applies. For n=5 the group may be a solvable subgroup of S5 (for example x5−2 is solvable by radicals, since 25 is already a radical), or all of S5, as for x5−4x+2. The degree alone does not decide.

This post completes the core course: from the integers and modular arithmetic (post 00), through groups, actions and Sylow theory (posts 01–03), rings and fields (post 04), to Galois theory. The table below lists the planned extensions. Each builds directly on the material here, so the series can grow without renumbering the existing posts.

Post · Topic · What it covers
06 · Modules and linear algebra over rings · Modules, free modules, the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID; the finite abelian groups of post 03 and the rational and Jordan canonical forms as two special cases
07 · Representation theory of finite groups · Group representations, Maschke's theorem, Schur's lemma, characters and orthogonality, character tables of S3, S4 and A5
08 · Algebraic number theory · Rings of integers, Dedekind domains, how unique factorisation of ideals repairs Z[−5], the class group, cyclotomic fields
09 · Commutative algebra and a first look at algebraic geometry · Noetherian rings, the Hilbert basis theorem, localisation, the Nullstellensatz, varieties and their coordinate rings
10 · Algebra in cryptography · Finite-field arithmetic in practice (AES uses F28), Diffie–Hellman and discrete logarithms, elliptic-curve groups, lattices and lattice-based cryptography

D. S. Dummit and R. M. Foote, Abstract Algebra, 3rd edition, Wiley, 2004 — Chapters 13 (field extensions, constructions, splitting fields, finite fields) and 14 (Galois theory, finite fields, Galois groups of polynomials, solvability by radicals).
M. Artin, Algebra, 2nd edition, Pearson, 2011 — Chapters 15 (fields, ruler and compass) and 16 (Galois theory, quintic equations).
I. Stewart, Galois Theory, 4th edition, CRC Press, 2015 — a readable, historically informed development, including Abel–Ruffini.
J. S. Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, course notes (free).
E. Artin, Galois Theory, Notre Dame Mathematical Lectures 2, 1942 (Dover reprint) — the classic linear-algebra approach to the Fundamental Theorem.
MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.702 Algebra II (Spring 2011) — lecture notes on fields and Galois theory.
K. Conrad, Expository papers ("blurbs") — short notes on Galois theory, including Galois groups of cubics and quartics.
